A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CCS-based analysis of CLIP attention heads despite the changed title and expanded scope. Text, equations, tables and figures are readable throughout. V1 ends with references; v2 includes Appendix A and additional head-list tables, all included in this comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original human–LLM agreement measurements, CCS distributions and pruning experiments on image classification, OOD classification and video retrieval.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results, revises the human–LLM agreement results and adds original race- and gender-bias evaluations on FairFace and SocialCounterFactuals.

M1.justification: V1 uses GPT-4o alone to judge span–concept consistency. V2 Section 3.2.3 requires unanimous agreement among GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5 Pro and Claude Sonnet, changing the scoring procedure. This is a limited component revision: TEXTSPAN extraction, five descriptions per head, ChatGPT concept labeling and soft-pruning remain.

E1.justification: V2 adds occupational race- and gender-bias evaluation on FairFace and SocialCounterFactuals, substantially extending the work into demographic-bias assessment. The five image-classification, two OOD and three video-retrieval datasets used in v1 are retained.

E2.justification: The existing random-pruning comparator is revised: v1 Section 5.3 describes selection without regard to learned properties, whereas v2 Section 4.2 explicitly excludes high-CCS heads. Unpruned, low-CCS and concept-specific pruning comparisons otherwise remain. The new bias experiments compare original models with high-CCS pruning.

E3.justification: The human-alignment study increases its reported sample from 50 to 100 TEXTSPAN descriptions. V2 also introduces a substantial bias-evaluation protocol using 104 occupations and four prompt templates, with MaxSkew at K=900 for FairFace and K=12 for race and K=4 for gender on SocialCounterFactuals. These are new evaluation settings, not comparable-setting performance improvements.

E4.justification: V2 Section 4.6 adds an ablation testing whether performance-important high-CCS heads also contribute to social bias, measuring race and gender skew before and after pruning on two datasets. This substantive analytical question is absent from v1. Existing OOD and concept-specific pruning analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Figure 2 changes its reported random-pruning average from three runs in v1 to five runs in v2; v2 Section 4.2 specifies five seeds. The plotted values remain unchanged, so this establishes a reporting change without independently confirming additional runs. Neither version supplies dispersion estimates or significance tests for these comparisons.

E6.justification: V2 adds demographic MaxSkew results in Tables 7–8 and individual head labels in Tables 10–12. Agreement scores also change: for ViT-B-32-OpenAI, Table 2 changes Kappa from 0.757 to 0.821 and Spearman correlation from 0.781 to 0.737 under revised judging and sample settings. Existing classification, OOD, video-retrieval and CCS-distribution numbers remain unchanged, including relocated and merged tables.

T1.justification: Although the displayed CCS summation retains its form, its indicator condition changes from acceptance by GPT-4o to unanimous acceptance by three judges. This is a limited revision to the metric's mathematical definition. CCS@K and the category thresholds remain unchanged, and no theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: V1 presents CCS principally as an interpretability metric identifying functionally important heads. V2's title, abstract, introduction and conclusion add a central performance–bias paradox: those heads allegedly encode spurious correlations and amplify social biases, while pruning them mitigates bias without fine-tuning. This substantially expands the claimed contribution.

C2.justification: V2 introduces a mechanism explanation linking contrastive training on uncurated data to demographic correlations encoded by high-CCS heads, and explicitly discusses a fairness–performance tradeoff. It also removes v1 Section 5.4's assertion that these heads avoid spurious correlations. Earlier architecture and concept-specialization interpretations are largely retained, including the discussion moved to Appendix A.

D1.justification: V2 Tables 10–12 provide full high-, medium- and low-CCS head lists with layer/head identifiers and concept labels for all six models, substantially improving documentation of pruning selections beyond v1's examples. Tables 5–6 additionally specify the complete occupation list and bias prompt templates, while Tables 7–8 disclose MaxSkew cutoffs.

R1.justification: V2 adds references to SocialCounterFactuals, VisoGender, DEAR and FairFace to ground its bias extension, plus Liu and Zhang on LLM-judge reliability. The OpenCLIP software citation is removed. These are limited literature additions and positioning changes; the existing interpretability-related-work discussion remains largely intact.

P1.justification: V2 substantially rewrites the introduction around social bias, condenses v1's Methodology into Section 3.1, consolidates the concept-specific pruning subsections, and moves the CCS-distribution discussion from Section 5.1 to Appendix A. The title, conclusion and several results paragraphs are also rewritten, producing substantial narrative and structural changes.

P2.justification: V2 adds occupation, prompt, bias-result and head-list tables; merges v1 Tables 5–6 into Table 4; relocates the CCS-distribution table to Appendix A; and compacts the agreement table. It also changes the document template and figure placement. The artwork and plotted values of Figures 1–5 are retained.

improvement.justification: V2 adds useful bias evidence, expands human validation and documents exact head selections. However, its new central claim that high-CCS heads are primary bias drivers lacks low-CCS or random-pruning controls on the bias tasks. Its claim of consistent reductions also conflicts with FairFace race MaxSkew increasing from 59.28 to 59.75 for ViT-L-14-OpenAI and SocialCounterFactuals gender MaxSkew increasing from 0.81 to 2.03 for ViT-B-16-OpenAI. The documentation gains and new evidential overreach leave the overall net quality change uncertain.
